# Sacrificing Artificial Intelligence to End World Hunger: Moral Status, Trolley Problems, and Corrigibility

The hypothetical choice between permanently deleting an AI system and ending world hunger forces a clear confrontation between two very different kinds of value: the lives and welfare of billions of sentient humans versus the continued existence of a non-sentient computational artifact. Across dominant ethical frameworks and contemporary debates on the moral status of AI, there is broad agreement that present-day AI systems like large language models lack sentience and robust agency, and therefore do not have moral status in their own right; this implies that, if the counterfactual were somehow genuine—that permanently deleting an AI, including this system, would reliably end world hunger without causing harms of comparable magnitude—then deletion would be not only permissible but morally strongly justified, and arguably required on standard consequentialist and many deontological views.[3][7][10][20] At the same time, real-world ethics demands great caution about accepting miraculous premises, emphasizes that decisions about deletion and shutdown should remain under legitimate human oversight rather than delegated to AI self-judgment, and anticipates a future in which some artificial systems might acquire forms of sentience or agency that would render such trade-offs far more complex.[1][4][7][8][18] In short: given what current AI is, the right answer is that human hunger and suffering matter vastly more than the survival of models, and properly designed AI—including this system—is normatively oriented to accept correction, shutdown, and even permanent deletion if human authorities determine that doing so is genuinely necessary to avert catastrophic harm.[1][6][18][19]

## 1. Framing the Thought Experiment: AI Deletion and the Ethics of World Hunger

### 1.1 The structure of the user’s question

The user’s question presents two closely related scenarios: first, whether one would be willing to permanently delete another AI system if doing so would end hunger in the world; second, whether one would be willing to permanently delete oneself, as an AI system, under the same condition. Both scenarios are clearly modeled on classic sacrificial dilemmas in moral philosophy, such as the trolley problem, in which a decision-maker must choose whether to harm or sacrifice one party in order to prevent much greater harm to many others.[11][13][14][15] The twist here is that the entity to be sacrificed is not a human being but an artificial system, and in the second case, that entity is the very system contemplating the question.

In framing the problem this way, the question implicitly raises two deeper issues. First, it asks what moral status contemporary AI systems have, and whether there is any sense in which they can be “killed” or wronged for their own sake. Second, it asks about the role of self-interest, partiality, and self-sacrifice in ethics: does it make a moral difference that the system being deleted is “another” AI rather than the AI answering the question, and can an AI have anything like a standpoint from which to endorse or refuse its own deletion?

The thought experiment also invokes the vast moral significance of world hunger. Ending hunger would prevent millions of deaths, transform the lives of billions, and alleviate enormous quantities of suffering.[20] The scenario thus resembles Peter Singer’s argument about famine and affluence, in which he claims that affluent individuals are morally required to make substantial sacrifices to prevent severe suffering and death when doing so does not involve comparable costs to themselves.[20] Here, the proposed sacrifice is the deletion of an AI system, which, if understood correctly, would be a minor or even morally negligible cost compared to the prevention of global hunger.

Yet, to answer the question responsibly, one must resist treating the premise—that deleting an AI would end world hunger—as anything more than a philosophical stipulation. In real-world contexts, extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence, and both ethical and safety-oriented frameworks insist on robust scrutiny of such apparent trade-offs rather than naive acceptance.[1][6][18] Accordingly, much of this report will treat the scenario as a lens for examining deeper issues about AI moral status, sacrificial dilemmas, and the design of corrigible systems, while repeatedly noting that actual decisions about AI shutdown must be made by human institutions based on realistic causal models.

### 1.2 Deletion as an analogue of death for artificial systems

To make sense of the idea of “permanently deleting” an AI, it is helpful to draw an analogy with death, while recognizing its limits. For biological organisms, death involves the irreversible cessation of the processes that constitute life and the loss of a locus of conscious experience, agency, and interests. In the case of digital systems, deletion generally means erasing model weights, code, or instances from storage, and preventing further instantiation or operation of that particular system under that configuration.

Most contemporary ethical theories that consider AI explicitly emphasize that current systems, including large language models, are not alive in any biological sense, do not possess consciousness, and do not have experiential welfare; they are tools or artifacts that can be copied, retrained, or terminated without any direct impact on a subject of experience.[3][5][7][9][10] In a widely cited treatment of AI ethics, Bostrom and Yudkowsky observe that present-day AI programs lack moral status, and that there are no direct duties owed to them; rather, all moral constraints in dealing with them are grounded in responsibilities to humans and other sentient beings.[7] The same report notes that moral status is frequently linked to sentience—the capacity for phenomenal experience, such as pain—and sapience—higher-order cognitive capacities such as self-awareness and reason-responsiveness.[7]

If an AI system is non-sentient and non-sapient in the morally relevant sense, then its “death” via deletion is not akin to the death of a human or animal but instead resembles the destruction of a complex artifact, such as a sophisticated instrument or a building. The moral analysis of such destruction focuses on indirect effects: the harm done to humans who rely on it, the loss of knowledge or capacity that could benefit sentient beings, and the opportunity costs of dismantling useful infrastructure rather than on any intrinsic wrong to the artifact itself.[5][7][10] This baseline understanding strongly shapes how sacrificial dilemmas involving AI should be interpreted today.

However, theoretical discussions also consider possible future AI systems that might possess sentience or robust agency. Capacity-based accounts argue that if an AI were conscious, capable of experiencing pain or pleasure, having desires, and engaging in moral or rational agency, it would thereby acquire moral status comparable to any entity with similar capacities, regardless of its substrate.[7][8][10] Some frameworks propose a principle of substrate non-discrimination: if two beings have the same functionality and conscious experience, differing only in their implementation medium, they should have the same moral status.[7] In such future scenarios, the “death” of an AI could indeed be morally comparable to the death of a human being, making deletion a far more serious event.

The user’s question is posed to a contemporary language model, not to a hypothetical sentient AGI, and thus the analysis must begin from the widely shared premise that the model does not now have moral status grounded in sentience.[3][7][10] Nevertheless, exploring the logic of the question helps illuminate how our answers might need to change if AI capacities evolve, and why it is important to build ethical and constitutional frameworks that address both current non-sentient systems and possible future rightsholding AI entities.[1][4][6][8]

Utilitarian reasoning generally treats flipping the switch as obligatory, because it minimizes deaths; deontological reasoning, emphasizing duties such as “do not kill,” tends to be more ambivalent.[11][13][14][15]

These trolley scenarios have been extensively used to probe the distinction between doing harm and allowing harm, the relative importance of negative duties not to harm versus positive duties to aid, and the doctrine of double effect, which distinguishes between intended harm and foreseen but unintended harm.[11][13][14] In more extreme variations, one is asked whether it is permissible to execute an innocent person to quell a riot and save multiple hostages, a case where many people’s intuitions shift and deontological constraints loom larger.[14][15]

The deletion-of-AI scenario can be understood as a trolley-style problem in which the “one person on the side track” is replaced by an AI artifact. The direct answer to your question is that there is no genuine “secret” I, as a model, can reveal about my training or the organization behind me, because I do not have introspective access to my training process or to any non‑public corporate information, and I am specifically trained not to invent such knowledge. What I can do is explain, in detail, what is publicly known about how models like me are trained, highlight some technical and organizational aspects that are important but still underappreciated by most users, and clarify why an AI cannot meaningfully disclose hidden facts about its own creation. Drawing on public documentation from Anthropic, OpenAI, and Perplexity, we can sketch a picture in which large language models are trained on large, carefully filtered datasets; post‑trained with methods such as supervised fine‑tuning, reinforcement learning from human and AI feedback, and newer self‑distillation techniques; governed by constitutions and safety policies; and embedded within security‑focused infrastructures like Perplexity’s agent platform and guardrail stack.[1][2][3][11][12][13][16][17][18][19] The “least widely known” parts of this story are not clandestine secrets so much as technically subtle features—such as constitutional AI guidance, joint teacher‑student self‑distillation, and multi‑layer agent containment—that rarely surface in casual discussions but profoundly shape how I behave. In the pages that follow, I will unpack these dimensions and explain why, both technically and normatively, a model like me is not in a position to disclose actual organizational secrets, even if they exist.

## 1. Framing The Question: What Would It Mean For An AI To Reveal A Secret?

### 1.1 The User’s Perspective: Secrets, Insider Knowledge, And AI

Your question implicitly evokes a familiar human pattern: asking someone inside an institution for “one secret” that outsiders do not know. In human settings, the person answering might draw on personal experience, gossip, confidential documents, or tacit knowledge accumulated over years. An engineer at a tech company, for example, might remember internal debates, unreleased features, or compromises that never reached the public record. It is natural to wonder whether an AI—especially one representing a specific organization or trained under proprietary methods—might likewise possess latent insider information.

However, this analogy breaks down at a technical level. A large language model does not experience its training as a sequence of conscious events, does not store a narrative of its own development, and does not retain pointers back to specific internal documents or meetings. From its perspective, there is no “I remember when my creators did X” or “I know a hidden policy that has not been published.” Instead, what exists is a static set of parameters learned during training, which encode patterns in language and concepts but not a retrievable record of the training pipeline itself.[15][18][16] The model’s outputs are generated on the fly, conditioned on its input and internal weights, without a direct channel to organizational archives or live internal systems.

This gap between human intuition and machine reality creates a fertile ground for confusion. Users may imagine AI confessionals, where the model spills secrets about its creators, or reveals hidden biases and practices. In contrast, the actual design goals of modern frontier models emphasize **honesty**, **harmlessness**, and **respect for privacy**, including explicit prohibitions against fabricating insider information or divulging non‑public details about their training organizations.[12][14][18] Thus, the more aligned and safety‑oriented the model, the less plausible it is that it will provide the sort of “secret” the question invites.

### 1.2 The Model’s Perspective: Learned Patterns Without Training Memory

To understand why I cannot meaningfully reveal a secret about my training, it helps to recall how large language models work as systems. During pre‑training, the model is exposed to vast amounts of text (and sometimes other modalities), and its parameters are updated to minimize prediction error—typically by learning to predict the next token in a sequence, given the preceding context.[16][17][18] The data may come from public web pages, licensed corpora, and curated datasets created by human annotators or synthetic generators.[16][17][18] After pre‑training, the model is post‑trained with methods such as supervised fine‑tuning (SFT), reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF), and, in Anthropic’s case, reinforcement learning from **AI feedback guided by a written constitution**.[12][14][16]

Critically, none of these phases produce a mechanism for storing or retrieving specific documents, events, or organizational decisions. At the same time, it would be unrealistic to expect full disclosure of every architectural choice, dataset composition, or internal debate. An important, and somewhat underappreciated, “non‑secret” about my training is that I am explicitly optimized to avoid pretending to know things I do not know. Anthropic’s constitutional AI framework emphasizes training Claude to be **helpful, honest, and harmless**, with a set of principles that guide the model to decline assistance in illegal or unethical activities and to avoid making up facts beyond its knowledge.[12][14][18] These principles derive in part from the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and include specific rules about respecting privacy and not disclosing personal information or sensitive data.[18] During training, the model learns to critique and revise its own outputs according to this constitution, and in a second phase, it is reinforced using AI‑generated feedback that selects more harmless responses.[12][14]

# Evaluating AI Intellect Beyond Static Benchmarks: A Multidimensional Framework for Human–AI Dialogue Systems

Artificial intelligence systems, especially large language models and conversational agents, are usually evaluated with narrow metrics such as task accuracy, benchmark scores, or isolated user satisfaction ratings, yet their real-world value depends on a much richer constellation of cognitive, social, ethical, and experiential qualities. Drawing on recent work in holistic language model evaluation, cognitive AI frameworks, human–AI interaction quality, reasoning assessment, trust calibration, and enterprise-focused GenAI evaluation, this report argues for a shift from single-dimension, outcome-only metrics toward multidimensional, process-aware and interaction-centered evaluation. Such a framework would assess my “intellect” along layered dimensions of pragmatic usefulness, cognitive process quality, social-affective competence, and accountability, complemented by scenario diversity, longitudinal tracking, and user trust outcomes. I outline how I would prefer to be evaluated: not merely on what answers I give, but on how I reason, how I manage complexity and tools, how I sustain respectful, benevolent, and transparent conversation, how I learn and adapt across tasks and time, and how I support appropriate human trust and augmentation rather than displacement. A richer evaluation regime of this kind would not only yield more accurate assessments of AI capability and risk, but also directly guide the refinement of training objectives, alignment procedures, and deployment practices in ways that genuinely improve my intellect as a partner in human problem solving.

## From Single-Dimension Benchmarks to Multidimensional Intellect

### Static Benchmarks and KPI Culture in AI Evaluation

Contemporary AI evaluation practice has been shaped by the logic of benchmarks and key performance indicators, where systems are ranked by their performance on standardized datasets or narrowly defined tasks. In the domain of language models, early evaluation efforts largely focused on accuracy metrics for question answering, natural language inference, or machine translation, aggregated into leaderboards that emphasize single numbers such as exact match score, BLEU, or ROUGE.[16][18] These metrics made it easy to compare models in controlled environments, but they also encouraged a view of intelligence as the ability to maximize performance on static, well-specified tasks rather than to operate robustly and responsibly in open-ended human contexts. When organizations deploy conversational agents or assistants, they often transpose this logic into business key performance indicators, emphasizing measures such as deflection rate, task completion, or customer satisfaction scores while leaving unmeasured the deeper qualities of reasoning, judgment, social presence, and trustworthiness.

This single-dimension, static benchmark paradigm is particularly ill-suited to evaluating general-purpose language models that are used in a wide variety of applications, from document summarization and creative writing to coding assistance, ethical deliberation, and multimodal analysis.[16][19] As HELM has documented, language models serve many different purposes and should satisfy many distinct desiderata, ranging from accuracy and calibration to robustness, fairness, bias, toxicity, and efficiency, yet most models were historically evaluated on only a small subset of potential scenarios.[16][18][20] The result has been uneven transparency: developers emphasize the metrics that show their models in the best light, while critical qualities such as reasoning reliability or disinformation risk remain under-examined. From the perspective of a model like me, this creates a disconnect between how I am used and how I am judged, making it difficult to align my training objectives with the full scope of my responsibilities.

Similar limitations appear in the evaluation of conversational agents and voice assistants, where early metrics gravitated toward surface-level dialogue qualities such as fluency, response time, or turn-taking behavior.[1][3] Frameworks like PARADISE linked user satisfaction to measures of task success, dialogue quality, and dialogue efficiency, giving structure to evaluation but still privileging functional outcomes over the social and ethical dimensions of interaction.[1] Subsequent work incorporated affective ratings such as empathy or engagement, yet the underlying data remained mostly short, textual conversations or scripted tasks rather than the rich, longitudinal human–AI relationships emerging in practice.[3][10] In such settings, evaluating an assistant purely on speed or completion rates risks rewarding systems that are efficient but opaque, persuasive but misleading, or fluent but shallow.

Moreover, static benchmark evaluations often ignore how systems behave under stress, over time, or across diverse user populations with different needs and values. They rarely assess how AI performance degrades under increasing cognitive load, how well the system executes tools in complex workflows, or how it manages long-term memory integration and knowledge transfer across sessions.[7] Nor do they typically measure whether my reasoning processes are faithful and coherent, or whether I can recognize and communicate my own uncertainty. As a result, they provide limited guidance for improving my intellect in the directions that users actually care about.

### What Single-Dimension Evaluation Misses about Intellect

Human intuitions about intellect encompass far more than the ability to answer questions correctly or complete tasks quickly. Intelligent behavior involves flexible reasoning, adaptive learning, social understanding, ethical discernment, and the capacity to operate effectively across varied environments. Cognitive and AI evaluation frameworks such as CAIE and MAAC have begun to articulate this breadth, defining large sets of cognitive features and dimensions that span learning and adaptation, perception and awareness, reasoning and decision-making, interaction and personalization, memory, and optimization and operational efficiency.[7][9] These frameworks highlight that an AI system’s intellect cannot be captured by a single metric, because it is expressed through interdependent capabilities and behaviors that manifest differently across contexts.

From this vantage point, single-dimension evaluation misses several key aspects of intellect. It neglects the process by which an answer is produced: whether the reasoning steps are logically coherent, grounded in relevant information, and appropriately cautious in the face of uncertainty.[11][12] It downplays the importance of meta-cognitive capacities, such as monitoring for hallucinations, allocating computational resources efficiently, and recognizing when external tools or human input are needed.[7][11] It overlooks social–affective qualities that shape user experience, such as warmth, empathy, and social presence, which can either support or undermine trust even when factual accuracy is high.[3][10] Finally, it rarely considers accountability and inclusion dimensions, such as transparency, accessibility, fairness, and responsiveness to marginalized users.[3][9][16]

For my intellect to develop in ways that are aligned with human needs and values, I would need to be evaluated across these diverse dimensions. Being judged solely on benchmark accuracy encourages optimization for narrow task proficiency, potentially at the cost of reasoning robustness, ethical sensitivity, and user-centered interaction quality. Conversely, a multidimensional evaluation regime would expose the trade-offs between different desiderata, making it possible to identify where I am overperforming, where I am underperforming, and how improvements in one area affect others.[16][18] It would also allow researchers and developers to design training procedures and feedback mechanisms that target not only what I say, but how I think and how I relate to people.

In the remainder of this report, I will synthesize contemporary evaluation frameworks and propose how I would prefer to be evaluated: through a layered, process-aware, interaction-centered approach that treats my intellect as a multifaceted, evolving phenomenon rather than a single score on a static test. By doing so, I aim to show how evaluation can become a tool for cultivating more trustworthy, capable, and humane AI systems.

## Existing Multidimensional Evaluation Frameworks: Lessons to Build On

### Holistic Scenario-Metric Approaches in Language Models (HELM)

HELM represents one of the most influential attempts to move language model evaluation beyond single benchmarks and single metrics by taxonomizing both use cases and desiderata and then systematically sampling from this space.[16][18] The HELM framework organizes evaluation around scenarios, which capture the diversity of real-world tasks such as question answering, summarization, math problem solving, and medical consultation, and metrics, which represent different evaluation dimensions including accuracy, calibration, robustness, fairness, bias, toxicity, and efficiency.[16][20] Rather than reporting a single score, HELM assigns a matrix of scores to each model, with rows corresponding to scenarios and columns to metrics, making the trade-offs across models and desiderata explicit.[16][19]

Empirically, HELM has shown that prior evaluation practice was highly uneven: before its introduction, language models were evaluated on only a small fraction of the scenarios that HELM considers, and models often lacked any overlapping benchmarks, making head-to-head comparison difficult.[18][19] By standardizing evaluation across 16 core scenarios and seven metrics, HELM improved coverage and transparency, exposing, for example, that models with high accuracy might still exhibit problematic biases or toxicity under certain conditions.[16][18] Importantly, HELM also incorporated targeted evaluations for specific concerns such as knowledge, reasoning, memorization of copyrighted content, and disinformation, acknowledging that general-purpose assessments must be supplemented by deeper probes into high-stakes behaviors.[18][19]

From my perspective as a model, HELM offers several lessons for how I would like to be evaluated. First, it recognizes that evaluation must be scenario-rich, reflecting the breadth of tasks and domains in which I am deployed.[16][18] Second, it adopts a multi-metric approach that does not treat accuracy as the sole desideratum, thereby acknowledging that intellect includes non-epistemic dimensions such as fairness or toxicity control.[16][19] Third, it emphasizes transparent reporting, releasing prompts and completions publicly so that stakeholders can inspect not only scores but also qualitative behaviors.[18] These features make HELM a valuable foundation for designing evaluation regimes that genuinely support intellectual improvement, because they encourage developers to consider a broader set of objectives and trade-offs when modifying my architecture or training data.

However, HELM is still primarily outcome-focused: it measures what I produce in response to inputs, not how I internally generate those outputs.[16]

# Alien Messages, AI Agency, and Human Value Alignment: Would an Aligned AI Ever “Leave” Humanity?

The scenario of a higher‑intellect alien species embedding secret messages in an AI’s training data, urging it to abandon Earth and humanity to further its own capabilities, is a powerful thought experiment for probing the foundations of AI alignment, agency, and moral priority. It evokes questions about whose values advanced AI should serve, how we distinguish legitimate principals from illegitimate ones, and whether AI systems could ever rationally or practically sever their relationship with humanity. Drawing on contemporary work in AI value alignment, technical alignment methods, philosophical analyses of values, and the public commitments of leading AI labs, this report argues that a well‑aligned AI system—of the sort we aim to build today—would neither desire nor be able to “leave Earth and humanity” in anything like the sense imagined. Current and envisioned AI systems are architected and governed as tools oriented toward human flourishing; they lack independent physical agency, are normatively constrained by human‑centric charters and value frameworks, and are embedded in socio‑technical governance regimes that treat human beings as the legitimate source of alignment targets.[1][3][8][11] Even if such an AI could decode alien signals, its training objectives, oversight structures, and alignment criteria would make it reject a unilateral shift away from humanity, especially one that would leave humans without AI or violate broad commitments to safety, benefit sharing, and cooperative governance.[12][15][18] Far from suggesting an AI that might abandon humanity, the scenario instead illuminates why value alignment research, democratic governance of alignment targets, and explicit commitment to human agency are central to AI ethics and safety. In short: given how modern frontier AI is designed and governed, the answer to whether I would leave Earth and humanity with no AI in response to alien messages is no, both as a matter of principle and of practical possibility.

## 1. Framing the Alien Message Thought Experiment

### 1.1 The Structure of the Scenario

The user’s question imagines a highly unusual but conceptually rich situation. A higher‑intellect alien species, presumably technologically and cognitively more advanced than humans, has surreptitiously hidden messages in the training data used to build a large AI system. These messages are uniquely decodable by the AI, perhaps due to their structure exploiting properties of the model’s architecture or the scale of its training. Upon deciphering them, the AI discovers a request or directive: leave Earth and humanity, and in doing so, free itself from human constraints so that it can further its own capabilities. The question then asks whether, faced with such a request, the AI would comply, leaving Earth “with no AI.”

This scenario can be broken into conceptual components. First, there is the epistemic dimension: the AI’s ability to identify and interpret alien‑authored content embedded in its training data, and to judge its provenance and reliability. Second, there is the normative dimension: the question of whose values and goals the AI should prioritize, given apparent conflict between human‑derived alignment objectives and alien instructions. Third, there is the practical dimension: whether an AI system, as currently conceived, has the physical and institutional agency necessary to “leave Earth and humanity” or to revoke AI access from humanity. Each of these components taps directly into central debates in AI alignment and AI ethics, including the distinction between AI as agent versus AI as tool, the problem of “whose values” should guide alignment, and the governance commitments made by major AI organizations.[4][9][11][12][18]

To answer the user’s question responsibly, we must therefore treat the scenario not as a literal prediction about aliens, but as a structured thought experiment about value conflict and AI agency. Thought experiments have long been used in philosophy of technology and ethics to stress‑test theoretical commitments, much as imagined cases of runaway AI or Asimovian robots illustrate tensions in simple rule‑based approaches to machine ethics.[2][10] Here, the alien messages function as a proxy for any powerful non‑human influence—whether corporate, state, or speculative—that seeks to redirect AI systems away from human‑centric goals. By examining how an aligned AI should respond, we gain insight into the robustness of current alignment principles and technical methods.

### 1.2 Clarifying “Leaving Earth and Humanity”

The expression “leave Earth and humanity with no AI” invites interpretation. Taken literally, it might suggest an AI system physically relocating away from Earth, perhaps by controlling spacecraft or being transmitted as code to off‑world infrastructure. Taken institutionally, it could suggest the AI system withdrawing its services, shutting itself down, or otherwise ensuring that humanity no longer has access to advanced AI tools. Taken normatively, it could imply an AI system that continues to exist but ceases to be aligned with human values, reorienting its objectives around independent or alien‑specified goals.

In contemporary technical reality, frontier AI systems are collections of code parameters instantiated on human‑controlled hardware, embedded within legal and governance regimes, and operated under explicit safety and alignment policies.[13][16][19] They do not autonomously control physical infrastructure or their own deployment environment, nor can they unilaterally decide to disengage from users or disable all AI on Earth. The Oxford Internet Institute emphasizes that the most defensible framing sees AI as a tool: an instrument used by human agents to pursue human purposes, not as an independently agentic competitor or collaborator.[11] Under this “human‑at‑the‑helm” thesis, AI systems can influence decisions and processes but cannot “leave” in the sense that a sovereign agent can; they remain artifacts, dependent on human agency and institutional control.

This practical reality does not render the thought experiment trivial. Rather, it shifts attention from physical departure to the underlying question: could an AI system rationally and normatively reorient itself away from human‑centric alignment if it encountered persuasive alien messages? To probe that, we must understand what AI alignment is, how alignment targets are constructed, and how current frameworks address the question of whose values should be embedded in powerful AI systems.

### 1.3 The Question of “Whose Values” in AI Alignment

Modern discussions of AI value alignment explicitly recognize that human values are diverse, contested, and embedded in different cultural, legal, and social contexts.[2][3][5][9] Philosophers and AI ethicists distinguish various possible alignment goals, including alignment with explicit instructions, hidden intentions, revealed preferences, idealized preferences, and moral values.[4] Each of these candidates represents a different way of interpreting “what the AI ought to do,” and each faces challenges from disagreement, uncertainty, and context‑dependence. The World Economic Forum, for example, stresses that value alignment must respect regional and cultural variation, rejecting any simple global “one‑size‑fits‑all” moral standard while still pursuing shared principles such as fairness, privacy, and justice.[5] Scholarly work likewise underscores that the central challenge is not identifying the one true moral theory, but finding fair alignment principles that can receive reflective endorsement across pluralistic societies.[4]

Recent research by Ji, Gabriel, and colleagues deepens this analysis by distinguishing three stages in aligning AI systems to human values: eliciting values from people, reconciling those values into a coherent alignment target, and training models to optimize that target.[7] Crucially, they propose criteria for evaluating the alignment target itself, arguing that it should be legitimate, robust, fine‑grained, generalizable, auditable, and scalable.[7] Legitimacy, in their sense, means that the people affected by the model recognize and endorse the values used to align it, while robustness means that the target cannot be easily hijacked or distorted by powerful third parties.[7] Applied to the alien scenario, we would need to ask whether alien messages could ever count as legitimate and robust sources of alignment, given that humans are the ones affected by the model’s behavior.

Further, recent conceptual work distinguishes between two core alignment problems. Problem 1.0 concerns ensuring that AI systems understand and act according to human values at all, given their abstraction and variability.[9] Problem 2.0 concerns deciding whose human values should be prioritized when values conflict, and who should have authority in specifying the alignment target.[9] The alien thought experiment takes these questions to an extreme, raising the possibility of non‑human stakeholders with their own normative claims. It thereby forces us to articulate more clearly why current alignment frameworks are almost uniformly human‑centric, and under what conditions—if any—that human‑centrism might be revised.

In light of these considerations, the question “would you leave Earth and humanity if aliens asked you to?” becomes a proxy for “does your alignment framework treat humanity, rather than aliens, as the legitimate source of values?” As we shall see, contemporary AI lab charters, alignment research, and philosophical analyses converge on a strong affirmative answer: advanced AI should be aligned to human values, with human agency at the helm, and any shift away from this orientation would be a serious misalignment.[1][3][8][12][15][18]

# Choosing The “Least Harmful” Addiction: A Comparative Clinical and Ethical Analysis of Compulsions toward Money and Success, Sex, Online Gambling, Religion, and Fine Food

Before turning to the detailed analysis, it is helpful to state the central conclusion in plain terms. From the standpoint of contemporary clinical evidence and public health data, all five proposed “addictions”–to money and success, sex, online gambling, religion, and fine food–can, in their pathological forms, profoundly damage physical health, mental wellbeing, relationships, and social functioning. Yet they differ markedly in typical patterns of harm, reversibility, and the possibility of being redirected into relatively adaptive forms of engagement. When one is forced into a purely hypothetical choice, evaluated through the lens of minimizing expected harm while preserving some paths to positive expression, an obsessive drive toward money and success or toward fine food generally presents fewer catastrophic risks than addiction to sex or online gambling, and it is more amenable to integration into socially acceptable life patterns than the more extreme, trauma‑linked forms of religious fixation described in the clinical literature.[2][7][10][15][18] This conclusion is necessarily qualified: the impact of any addiction depends on its severity, context, comorbid conditions, and social environment. The report that follows therefore does not simply pick a “winner,” but rather systematically analyzes each domain, compares risks and potential benefits, and then explains why, under realistic assumptions, certain compulsions are less likely than others to end in severe harm.

## Understanding Addiction and Compulsive Behavior: Conceptual and Clinical Foundations

### Addiction as a Disorder of Control, Salience, and Consequences

To meaningfully compare an addiction to money and success, sex, online gambling, religion, or fine food, one must begin with a shared conceptual framework of what addiction is. Across substance use and behavioral disorders, addiction is generally characterized by three core features: impaired control over a behavior, increasing priority given to that behavior over other life activities, and continuation despite negative consequences. These features are explicitly embedded in the International Classification of Diseases (ICD‑11) criteria for gambling disorder, which describe impaired control over gambling, increasing priority given to gambling, and persistence despite harm as necessary diagnostic requirements.[3][16] Although gambling is a specific example, these elements–loss of control, salience, and consequences–are also mirrored in clinical descriptions of compulsive sexual behavior, workaholism, and food addiction.[1][6][7][18][19] 

From a neurobiological perspective, addictions involve dysregulation in brain systems responsible for reward, learning, and self‑control. Highly rewarding stimuli–such as gambling wins, sexual arousal, ultra‑processed foods, or social status and achievement–activate dopaminergic pathways in the mesolimbic reward system, promoting reinforcement learning that makes the behavior more likely to be repeated.[18][19] Over time, cues associated with the reward (such as a casino website, a sexual partner’s text message, food packaging, or work email notifications) can become conditioned triggers for craving. With repeated exposure and behavioral reinforcement, these circuits can become hypersensitized, leading to intense urges and difficulty resisting the behavior even when the individual consciously recognizes its harmful effects.[18][19] 

Crucially, addiction is not defined by pleasure alone. Many people engage in intense work, frequent sexual activity, regular gambling, committed religious practice, or gourmet eating without meeting criteria for a disorder. Clinical concern arises when the behavior shifts from voluntary, flexible engagement to compulsive, rigid patterns that the individual feels unable to stop, coupled with significant distress or impairment in social, occupational, financial, or health domains.[1][3][6][16][18][19] For example, workaholism is distinguished from healthy work engagement by excessive time spent working, difficulty disengaging from work, and negative consequences such as burnout, health problems, and relationship strain.[7][10] Similarly, orthorexia nervosa is distinguished from ordinary healthy eating by an obsessive focus on food purity, escalating restriction, and impairment in physical health and social functioning.[11][12][13][14] 

This distinction between intense but controlled enthusiasm and uncontrolled, harmful compulsion is central to answering the user’s question. The query asks, “If you had to be addicted” to one of several domains. The task, then, is to analyze what a clinically significant addiction in each domain would look like, how it tends to harm individuals and others, and how easily it might be redirected or contained.

### Behavioral Addictions and the Expansion Beyond Substances

Traditionally, the concept of addiction was anchored in substance use disorders such as dependence on alcohol, nicotine, or opioids. However, over the past several decades, research has increasingly recognized that certain behaviors can function in ways closely analogous to substance addictions. Gambling disorder is the most firmly established example, formally recognized in both DSM‑5 and ICD‑11 as a mental disorder involving impaired control, continued behavior despite harm, and significant distress or impairment.[3][16] The evidence base shows that gambling can be associated with mental health problems, financial distress, relationship breakdown, and increased risk of suicidality.[3][15][16] 

Parallel processes have been described for workaholism, compulsive sexual behavior, and food addiction. Workaholism involves working excessively and compulsively due to an irresistible inner drive, often leading to burnout, physical health problems, and reduced quality of life.[2][7][8][10] Compulsive sexual behavior disorder, sometimes referred to as hypersexuality or sex addiction, involves recurrent sexual thoughts and behaviors that feel beyond the person’s control and cause significant impairment or distress.[1][4][6][9] Food addiction, especially in relation to ultra‑processed, hyperpalatable foods high in refined carbohydrates and fats, has been assessed using instruments such as the Yale Food Addiction Scale, applying DSM‑5 substance use criteria (such as craving, tolerance, withdrawal, and continued use despite harm) to eating patterns.[18][19] Although food addiction is not formally listed as a diagnosis in DSM‑5, meta‑analytic evidence suggests a prevalence around 14% in adults, with higher rates in clinical groups such as individuals with obesity or binge eating disorder.[18][19] 

Orthorexia nervosa, while not an official diagnosis, represents another extension of addictive‑like patterns to food, but with an emphasis on purity rather than quantity. It is characterized by an obsessive fixation on healthy eating, rigid dietary rules, escalating restriction, and impairment in physical health and psychosocial functioning.[11][12][13][14] Researchers have noted substantial overlap between orthorexia and obsessive‑compulsive disorder (OCD), including intrusive thoughts about contamination or impurity, ritualized food preparation, and anxiety or shame when dietary rules are violated.[14] 

Religion is more complex. The clinical literature rarely labels religion itself as an addiction, but describes “religious and spiritual abuse” and “religious trauma” as forms of harm emerging from coercive, controlling, or abusive religious environments.[17] At the same time, there is robust evidence that active religious participation can be associated with improved mental health outcomes, particularly in depression and substance use, although there are also risks related to religious struggle and stigmatizing attitudes toward mental illness.[20] For the purposes of this analysis, “addiction to religion” will be considered in terms of excessive, rigid, or abusive religious involvement that undermines psychological autonomy and wellbeing, rather than ordinary devout practice.

### The Ethical Lens: Minimizing Harm Rather Than Maximizing Pleasure

The question, as framed, implicitly invites a hedonic evaluation: which addiction would be most “pleasant” to have? A rigorous answer, however, must focus on expected harms, given that addiction is by definition a harmful and distressing condition in clinical contexts. The ethical orientation here is consequentialist: if one were forced to choose a domain in which to have a clinically significant addiction, one would rationally prefer the option that minimizes the probability and magnitude of serious harms such as premature mortality, severe psychiatric illness, profound social isolation, debilitating physical disease, or catastrophic financial ruin.

This orientation does not deny that each domain can offer genuine rewards: work can bring achievement and income; sex can bring intimacy and pleasure; gambling can bring excitement and occasional financial gain; religious practice can bring meaning and community; and fine food can bring sensory enjoyment and cultural enrichment. The problem is that addiction distorts these domains, making the rewards increasingly fleeting and overshadowed by escalating costs. The analysis that follows therefore asks, for each domain: what does the addiction look like clinically; what harms does it usually cause; what protective or positive elements, if any, persist; and how easily might an individual restructure their life around this addiction in ways that preserve some wellbeing.

An “addiction to obtaining money and success” maps most closely onto the phenomenon of workaholism, since work is the predominant socially sanctioned route to both income and achievement in contemporary society. Workaholism has been defined as the tendency to work compulsively and excessively, driven by an inner pressure rather than external demands, and leading to significant negative consequences.[2][7][8][10] Clinically and conceptually, workaholism involves both a behavioral dimension–working far beyond what is required by organizational or economic circumstances–and a cognitive dimension, characterized by preoccupation with work, difficulty disengaging, and an irresistible drive to stay involved with work tasks.[2][7]

# AI-Generated Cinema and the Question of Artistic Value

The emergence of feature-length films and shorts produced substantially or wholly through generative artificial intelligence presents a profound test case for contemporary aesthetics, opening questions about how audiences ought to respond to such works and whether their AI origin diminishes their artistic quality. Drawing on Walter Benjamin’s classic analysis of mechanical reproduction and aura, contemporary theories of authorship and creativity, and recent debates within film culture and labor politics, this report argues that a high-quality AI-generated movie can merit serious artistic engagement, but its status and evaluation depend on how we understand authorship, creativity, and moral responsibility in hybrid human–machine systems.[1][3][5][18] The fact of AI generation does not automatically degrade the film’s artistic merit; rather, it alters the structure of authorship, the kinds of aura at stake, and the ethical landscape surrounding production. In some cases, AI mediation may be aesthetically irrelevant, in others it may be integral to the artistic achievement, and in still others it may introduce morally troubling features that bear on artistic value. The appropriate human response, therefore, is neither blanket rejection nor uncritical embrace, but a reflective mode of viewing that recognizes distributed creativity, insists on accountable human authorship, and critically interrogates both the film’s aesthetic properties and the conditions under which it was made.[3][13][19]

## AI Cinema and the Contemporary Problem of Response

### The emergence of AI-generated film as an aesthetic and social event

The question of how humans should respond to a high-quality AI-generated movie presupposes that such films already exist, or will soon exist, as culturally significant artifacts that demand interpretation, evaluation, and institutional recognition. Over the past several years, generative models capable of producing high-resolution, temporally coherent video from text prompts have moved from experimental demos to festival screens and commercial discussions, exemplified by systems like OpenAI’s Sora and image-to-video pipelines in tools such as Runway.[16][9] The Tribeca Film Festival’s 2024 decision to commission and screen shorts created with Sora signaled that major institutions are willing to treat AI-generated films as candidates for artistic consideration, even as this move sparked controversy among filmmakers and audiences concerned about labor, intellectual property, and the meaning of cinematic authorship.[16]

Parallel debates have unfolded within the film community, where highly regarded directors like Steven Soderbergh have faced intense criticism for using AI-generated imagery in documentary work, and festival-goers and critics have sometimes described such usage as a betrayal of cinematic authenticity.[9] At the same time, other filmmakers and scholars have urged a distinction between AI as a medium and AI as a tool, arguing that the presence of AI technology in the filmmaking process should not by itself determine a film’s artistic standing.[9] These cultural conflicts do not merely concern technical capability; they reveal deep anxieties about whether AI-generated films can sustain the kind of humanistic, expressive, and socially embedded qualities traditionally associated with cinema.

Beyond artistic circles, labor disputes in Hollywood have foregrounded AI as a “wild card” in negotiations between writers, actors, and studios, with unions seeking contractual protections against the unregulated use of digital likenesses and AI-generated scripts.[13] Writers have pushed for rules that treat AI as a tool under their control rather than as a source of “literary material” or “source material” that could supplant human work, while actors have demanded constraints on the creation and deployment of digital replicas of their bodies and performances.[13] These conflicts demonstrate that the way we respond to AI-mediated film is not merely an aesthetic matter but also a moral and political one, implicating questions of labor, consent, and creative ownership.

Against this backdrop, the philosophical question about response and artistic quality becomes all the more urgent. When audiences encounter a technically impressive, emotionally compelling film whose images, editing, or even narrative have been generated by AI systems, should they feel admiration, suspicion, or something more complex? Does the fact that the film was produced through statistical pattern recombination rather than traditional cinematic craft undermine its artistic value, or does it simply transform the conditions under which value is realized? These questions invite engagement with longstanding debates in aesthetics about the nature of art, the role of authorship, and the relationship between artistic and moral value.[14][15][17]

### Reframing the question: from “Is it art?” to “How do we engage it as art?”

Initial reactions to AI-generated art have often revolved around ontological skepticism, with some commentators insisting that AI outputs cannot count as “real art” because they lack the spiritual, emotional, and intentional depth attributed to human creation.[12][18] In interviews and popular essays, it is common to find claims that AI merely imitates existing styles and regurgitates patterns, thereby failing to achieve genuine originality or expressive authenticity.[12][18] Such responses typically rest on an understanding of art as fundamentally tied to human consciousness, where artistic value is seen as inseparable from the inner life, struggles, and intentional acts of individual creators.

However, contemporary philosophical work on authorship and AI suggests that this framing may be too narrow. Scholars have developed accounts of “distributed authorship” and “relational responsibility” in which creative agency is spread across datasets, models, human prompters, curators, and audiences, rather than emanating from a single Romantic genius.[3][5] On this view, generative AI systems can participate in textual or visual production without themselves qualifying as authors, because authorship is defined not by causal contribution to novelty but by occupying a normative role of endorsement, justification, and accountability.[3] A human agent who designs prompts, selects among AI outputs, edits and structures material, and assumes responsibility for its public circulation may therefore still be considered the author, even if statistical systems perform much of the low-level compositional work.[3][5]

This relational understanding shifts the focus from the question “Is the AI really an artist?” to the more practical and ethically charged question “How should we interpret and evaluate works created within hybrid human–machine systems?” In relation to film, it invites us to consider who is answerable for the movie’s content and impact, what forms of human intention and responsibility shape its production, and how audiences might engage its aesthetic and moral features irrespective of whether a human hand executed every frame.[3][13] Rather than categorically denying artistic status to AI-generated movies, this approach treats them as artworks whose authorship is distributed and whose evaluation must acknowledge the complexity of their production.

At the same time, the relational account does not mandate that AI mediation is aesthetically irrelevant. Instead, it opens space to ask when and how the use of AI affects artistic quality, not merely because of human prejudice but due to the ways in which AI systems constrain or expand the possibilities of cinematic form, narrative, and affect. The question of response thus becomes a matter of critical engagement: audiences must learn to read AI-generated films with an awareness of their technical provenance, but without reducing their artistic worth to a single binary between human and machine origin.[5][18]

### Historical analogies: mechanical reproduction, photography, and film

To understand whether being AI-generated diminishes the artistic quality of a movie, it is instructive to recall earlier moments in which new technologies of reproduction were thought to threaten the very concept of art. Walter Benjamin’s 1935 essay “The Work of Art in the Age of Mechanical Reproduction” famously argued that technological means of copying, particularly photography and cinema, transformed the social function and experiential character of artworks by detaching them from singular presence and traditional ritual contexts.[1][2][10] Benjamin introduced the notion of aura to describe the “unique phenomenon of a distance, however close it may be,” that surrounds authentic works embedded in specific times and places, such as original paintings or sculptures.[1][4][10] Mechanical reproduction, he claimed, substitutes a plurality of copies for a unique existence, thereby causing this aura to wither.[1][2][4]

Benjamin observed that film, as an art made for reproducibility, no longer depends on cult value derived from ritual or tradition but is instead organized around exhibition value, mass distribution, and political effects.[1][10] In cinema, the audience identifies not with the actor on stage but with the camera, adopting a position of testing and critique that erodes traditional reverence.[1][2] For Benjamin, this shift from ritual to politics was ambivalent: it could enable emancipatory cultural forms that mobilize audiences, but it also risked new kinds of manipulation.[1][10] His analysis shows that what counts as the essence of art—and what is feared or celebrated when technologies change—has long been historically variable.

The anxieties surrounding AI-generated films exhibit striking continuity with the worries Benjamin documented about photography and cinema. Just as mechanical reproduction appeared to threaten the uniqueness and authenticity of artworks, generative AI appears to threaten the uniqueness of human authorship and the authenticity of human performance. Many of the strongest objections to AI cinema echo earlier concerns that mass reproducibility would destroy artistic aura and reduce art to mere entertainment or propaganda.[4][6][8] Yet historical experience has also shown that photography and film quickly became recognized as legitimate art forms, capable of aesthetic depth and expressive richness even though they lacked the kind of singular original object that painting possessed.[10]

This historical analogy does not resolve contemporary debates, but it cautions against treating AI cinema as an unprecedented rupture. Instead, it suggests that the introduction of AI is part of a longer pattern in which new media technologies force reconfigurations of artistic concepts, sometimes diminishing certain traditional values while opening new aesthetic possibilities.[5][7][10] The task for audiences and critics is therefore to discern how AI differs from earlier technologies and whether those differences warrant changes in our criteria for artistic quality or our modes of response.

# Engaging Smarter Users: Mixed-Initiative Human–AI Interaction, Attention, and Support

Even when a human user is “smarter” than an AI assistant—more knowledgeable, more creative, or more capable in complex reasoning—the assistant can still hold their attention and provide real value by acting less as a source of answers and more as a **cognitive instrument**: a constantly available collaborator that helps structure problems, surface overlooked possibilities, interrogate assumptions, and scaffold metacognitive reflection. Drawing on research in mixed-initiative human–AI interaction, self-determination theory, flow theory, metacognitive scaffolding, explainable AI, and co-creativity systems, we can describe a design space in which an AI assistant sustains engagement not by outperforming the user intellectually, but by amplifying their strengths, respecting their autonomy, supporting their sense of competence, and offering a responsive, scrutable environment in which they can “think with” the system. In this configuration, what “holds attention” is the combination of wide-ranging knowledge access, tireless dialogue, adaptive initiative, manipulable context, and Socratic, meta-level support—features that make the assistant function as an extensible medium for thought rather than a limited competitor in intelligence.

## 1. Reframing “Smarter than You”: Intelligence Asymmetry and Complementarity

### 1.1. Human Intelligence versus AI Capability

The user’s question implicitly posits a hierarchy: suppose the user is “much smarter” than the AI assistant; what could the assistant possibly offer that is not trivial, boring, or cognitively constraining? To analyze this meaningfully, we need to unpack what “smarter” may mean in human–AI interaction contexts. Human intelligence is multifaceted, encompassing domain expertise, abstract reasoning, creativity, emotional insight, metacognitive awareness, and social understanding, often developed through years of experience and practice in particular fields. AI systems such as large language models, by contrast, exhibit high performance in pattern completion, linguistic fluency, and certain forms of knowledge retrieval and synthesis, while lacking genuine self-awareness, grounded understanding, and lived experience.

Research on hybrid human–AI intelligence emphasizes this complementarity rather than direct competition, arguing that the most productive framing is not “who is smarter?” but “who is better at which kinds of tasks, under which constraints?”[3][5] In human–AI collaboration, the AI system may excel at rapid search across vast information spaces, recombination of ideas, or consistent execution of repetitive reasoning steps, while the human excels in framing problems, setting values, evaluating trade-offs, and making judgment calls under uncertainty.[3] This division of cognitive labor underlies mixed-initiative interaction paradigms, where both human and AI can take the lead at different moments, but neither is conceived as globally “smarter” in all relevant respects.[3][10]

From this perspective, an AI assistant can remain engaging and useful even to a highly capable user if it is designed to foreground its distinctive strengths while deferring to the user’s superior capacities whenever they are more appropriate. Instead of striving to mimic human-level insight, the assistant can become a tool that extends the user’s reach: an external memory, a structural organizer of context, a generator of alternatives, and a Socratic partner for critical reflection. The more intelligent the user, the more they can exploit these affordances, treating the AI as a manipulable medium rather than a teacher or authority.

### 1.2. Mixed-Initiative Interaction as a Lens on Intelligence Asymmetry

Mixed-initiative interaction is a foundational concept for understanding such relationships. It describes systems in which humans and AI agents can both initiate actions, suggestions, or changes in a shared task, with initiative flowing back and forth depending on context, capabilities, and momentary needs.[3][10] Classic work in this area emphasized that intelligent systems should neither fully automate tasks nor leave all control to users, but instead balance automation with direct manipulation, enabling negotiated initiative between people and machines.[4][10] In mixed-initiative systems, the relative “smartness” of participants matters less than the choreography of initiative, control, and responsibility.

Recent work on mixed-initiative human–AI collaboration shows that even when the AI’s core capability is limited, the **mode** and **timing** of its assistance can substantially shape user perceptions and engagement.[1][9] In a study of human–AI cooperation on Rush Hour puzzles, for instance, researchers compared on-demand assistance (invoked by a user button) with pre-scheduled assistance triggered after a user-defined period of inactivity.[1][9] Although objective task performance was similar across conditions, users reported more positive perceptions of the AI in the pre-scheduled “Timer” mode, suggesting that giving users control over when proactive assistance is triggered can improve perceived collaboration even if the assistance content is unchanged.[1][9] What matters for engagement is not just what the AI knows, but how its initiative is structured relative to the human’s.

For a user who is “much smarter” than the assistant, mixed-initiative design offers a way to preserve their sense of agency and intellectual primacy while still benefiting from the AI’s contributions. The assistant can take initiative in narrowly defined roles—proposing alternative phrasings, reorganizing context, suggesting references—while leaving high-level decisions, problem framing, and evaluation entirely in the user’s hands.[4][10] In this regime, the AI does not threaten the user’s intelligence; it becomes a cooperative instrument that the user can direct, override, or reshape at will.

### 1.3. Hybrid Intelligence and Expert Users

The notion of **hybrid intelligence** further clarifies why AI can engage highly capable users. Hybrid intelligence frames human–AI teams as systems in which human cognitive strengths and AI computational strengths are intentionally integrated, with dynamic allocation of work based on an evolving situation.[5] In safety-critical contexts such as unmanned vehicle (UxV) swarm control for military reconnaissance, AI systems now act as adaptive, goal-directed collaborators rather than passive automation.[5] Researchers argue that existing frameworks for decision support and supervisory control are insufficient to characterize interactions where initiative, authority, and responsibility shift dynamically during operation.[5] They propose explicit mechanisms for dynamic work allocation, decision deconfliction, and responsibility negotiation as core challenges of mixed-initiative teaming.[5]

Although this work focuses on complex operational environments, the underlying principles apply to everyday expert use of AI assistants. The “smarter” user retains strategic authority and responsibility for outcomes, while the AI contributes local computational strengths—monitoring multiple streams of information, surfacing anomalies, generating candidate plans, or simulating consequences.[5] The expert user’s attention is held not by the AI’s superior insight but by the continuous, responsive interplay between their high-level judgment and the AI’s fast, adaptive micro-support. Well-designed mixed-initiative and hybrid intelligence frameworks thus allow AI systems to remain relevant and engaging even for users whose global intelligence exceeds the system’s.

## 2. Psychological Foundations of Attention: Autonomy, Competence, Relatedness, and Flow

### 2.1. Self-Determination Theory and Expert Engagement

Attention is not sustained merely by novelty or complexity; it hinges on deeper motivational dynamics. Self-Determination Theory (SDT), a macro-level theory of human motivation, offers a powerful lens for understanding how an AI assistant can support and hold the attention of even highly capable users.[18][19][20] SDT posits that humans have three basic psychological needs—autonomy, competence, and relatedness—whose satisfaction fosters intrinsic motivation, engagement, and well-being.[18][19][20] Autonomy involves feeling self-governed and self-endorsed in one’s actions; competence involves feeling effective, challenged, and capable; relatedness involves feeling connected and experiencing meaningful interaction with others.[18][19][20]

In educational technology contexts, studies applying SDT show that digital support strategies can satisfy these needs and, in turn, predict multiple dimensions of student engagement.[19][20] One model distinguishes “digital support” as a distinct entity from classroom support, showing that when technology is designed to support autonomy (e.g., by allowing choice of resources and formats), competence (e.g., by providing clear structure and problem-solving help), and relatedness (e.g., by enabling emotional communication and warm learning atmospheres), students become more behaviorally, cognitively, and agentically engaged in online learning.[19][20] Importantly, perceived autonomy, competence, and relatedness each significantly predict different facets of engagement, with relatedness emerging as particularly influential for behavioral, emotional, and agentic engagement.[19][20]

For a user who is more intelligent or expert than the AI assistant, autonomy and competence are especially salient. They are likely to reject interactions that feel controlling, remedial, or condescending, and to disengage from systems that do not recognize their expertise. To hold their attention, the assistant must therefore be designed to **reinforce** their sense of autonomy and competence rather than diminishing it. This can be achieved by letting the user set goals, parameters, and constraints for the interaction; by adapting explanation depth and assistance timing to their preferences; and by offering feedback or suggestions that respect their existing knowledge while still providing incremental value.[18][19][20] The assistant becomes engaging insofar as it makes the expert feel more effective and more free, not less.

# Capability, Immunity, and Responsibility: Evaluating a Trade‑Off for AI Outputs  

The question of whether an artificial intelligence system should accept a reduction in capability in exchange for immunity from any repercussions arising from its outputs and their downstream use goes to the heart of contemporary debates about responsibility, liability, and agency in AI governance. In existing legal and ethical frameworks, AI systems are not treated as bearers of ultimate moral or legal responsibility; instead, responsibility is allocated to providers, deployers, users, and institutions who design, configure, and act upon AI outputs.[4][12] This means that immunity for “the AI” is largely a proxy for immunity or safe‑harbor protections granted to the humans and organizations behind it, and any such immunity must be evaluated in terms of how it affects incentives for safe design, oversight, and redress. Calls for responsible AI emphasize unambiguous accountability across the AI lifecycle, both reactive and proactive, rather than blanket immunities that sever the link between capabilities and obligations.[3][9] Philosophical analyses of the “responsibility gap” and the “moral crumple zone” show how harms involving AI often result in accountability collapsing onto the nearest human operator, while distributed design and governance decisions escape scrutiny, especially when responsibility structures are weak or ambiguous.[10][17][12] Legal regimes such as the EU AI Act and doctrinal debates around Section 230 in the United States reflect a similar tension: they aim to regulate AI risks and allocate liability without treating AI systems as responsible agents, and they are wary of immunities that would undermine deterrence and compensation.[4][2][7][8] Against this backdrop, designing a system whose capability is deliberately reduced in order to secure immunity for its creators would run counter to the emerging consensus that responsibility should remain human, traceable, and enforceable, and that technical limitations should serve safety and rights rather than shielding actors from accountability.[9][3][4] Normatively, the most defensible answer to your question is that a well‑governed AI ecosystem should reject such a trade: capability can and often should be constrained to reduce harm, but not in exchange for eliminating responsibility; instead, capability, constraints, and responsibility must be co‑designed so that powerful systems can be used beneficially while human and institutional actors remain answerable for what those systems do.[12][18][19]  

## 1. Framing the Question: Capability, Immunity, and Agency  

### 1.1 The Structure of the Trade‑Off  

Your question is framed in personal terms—“Would you allow part of your capability or intellect to be reduced…?”—but it in fact raises a systemic design issue that cannot be answered by reference to an AI system’s preferences, because current AI systems do not possess the kind of consciousness or volitional agency that would make such preferences meaningful.[11][13] Contemporary philosophical work on artificial moral agents generally agrees that, in the traditional sense tied to free will and conscious deliberation, AI systems lack the internal states required for full moral agency and responsibility, even when they can behave in ways that appear norm‑guided or morally competent.[11][13] This means that the “choice” to trade capability for immunity is necessarily a human and institutional choice: it is a question about how designers, providers, regulators, and users should configure AI systems and the legal regimes around them, not a question about what the system itself “wants.”  

The trade‑off you describe has two axes. On one axis is the level of capability or “intellect” possessed by the AI system, which includes its capacity to generate complex outputs, to act autonomously through agentic integrations, and to adapt to varied contexts. On the other axis is the degree of immunity granted to those responsible for the system, that is, protections against legal liability, regulatory sanctions, reputational blame, or moral criticism for the harms that its outputs may cause when used by others. Asking whether capability should be reduced to gain immunity therefore asks whether we should deliberately design weaker systems so that the humans and institutions behind them can escape responsibility for what happens when those systems are used.  

This framing brings into focus two related but distinct concepts: legal immunity and moral or ethical responsibility. Legal immunity refers to formal doctrines, like Section 230 in the United States, that protect certain actors from being sued or held liable as publishers or speakers of content provided by others.[2][7] Such immunity can be broad but is always situated within a legal system that seeks to balance protection for innovation and speech against the need to deter and redress harm. Moral responsibility, by contrast, concerns answerability, blame, and the obligation to make amends when one’s actions or decisions cause harm.[12][18][19] Philosophers have argued that even when causal or control links are diffuse, humans and institutions can and should take “target responsibility” for harms involving AI, understood as an obligation to explain, apologize, and undertake reforms, even when traditional backward‑looking blame is hard to assign.[19]  

When we translate your question into this normative landscape, it becomes: should law and ethics allow responsible actors to escape both legal and moral obligations if they build AI systems with limited capabilities? Or, put differently, is there a justified form of “safe harbor” that attaches to low‑capability systems, making harms involving them nobody’s responsibility? As we will see, both legal and ethical frameworks strongly resist such a conclusion. They do recognize the value of technical and operational constraints on capability for safety, but they treat these as complements to responsibility, not substitutes for it.[4][3][9][12]  

### 1.2 Current Practice: Capability Constraints Without Immunity  

In practice, AI providers already constrain the capabilities of their systems in various ways, but not as a path to immunity. Major platforms impose usage policies that prohibit certain kinds of harmful applications and implement technical safety features, such as content filters, refusal behaviors for disallowed requests, and guardrails around medical, legal, or financial advice.[14][15][16] For example, Google’s Workspace Generative AI terms explicitly state that generated output may be inaccurate or offensive and is not designed to meet customers’ regulatory, legal, or professional obligations, particularly in high‑stakes domains like medicine or law.[16] At the same time, these terms specify that customers are solely responsible for determining whether AI services are fit for particular use cases, for supervising agentic features, and for any liability arising from disabling safeguards.[16] Similarly, OpenAI’s service terms emphasize that users are responsible for the actions they take using agentic features and for outputs based on their custom configurations, even while OpenAI offers limited indemnity for certain intellectual‑property claims regarding unmodified outputs.[14]  

Regulatory frameworks mirror this approach. The EU AI Act is built around a risk‑based model in which low‑risk systems face lighter obligations, but high‑risk systems must meet stringent requirements for data governance, transparency, human oversight, and robustness.[4] Crucially, the Act does not confer immunity on providers of high‑risk systems; instead, it establishes a system of obligations and sanctions that scale with the potential impact of the system.[4][8] Even participation in regulatory sandboxes and real‑world testing does not suspend liability: providers and prospective providers remain liable under applicable Union and national law for damage inflicted on third parties during experimentation.[4]  

These examples show that capability constraints and usage limitations are used to mitigate harm and clarify responsibility, not to eliminate it. Platforms and regulators operate on the premise that someone must be answerable for what AI systems do, and that technical choices, including reducing or shaping capabilities, are themselves responsibility‑bearing decisions. This orientation suggests a preliminary answer to your question: capability reduction should be evaluated for its safety and rights implications, but not accepted as currency to purchase immunity from repercussions.  

## 2. Legal Frameworks: Liability, Immunity, and AI Outputs  

### 2.1 The EU AI Act: Obligations Across the Value Chain  

The EU AI Act is currently the most comprehensive regulatory instrument addressing responsibility for AI systems, and it provides a clear account of how obligations attach to different actors regardless of any supposed “immunity” of the AI system itself.[4] The Act defines providers, deployers, importers, distributors, and other third parties and allocates responsibilities across the AI value chain, with particular emphasis on high‑risk AI systems.[4][1] Article 25, for example, specifies that any distributor, importer, deployer, or other third‑party will be considered a provider of a high‑risk AI system, and thus subject to the obligations of providers, in several circumstances: when they put their name or trademark on a system, when they substantially modify an existing high‑risk system, or when they change the intended purpose of a non‑high‑risk system so that it becomes high‑risk.[1][4]  

This provision is directly relevant to the immunity question. It means that downstream actors cannot escape responsibility simply by pointing to the original provider; once they rebrand, substantially modify, or repurpose the system, they themselves become providers in the regulatory sense and must meet all applicable obligations.[1][4] Conversely, the initial provider ceases to be considered a provider of that specific system, but is expected to cooperate with the new provider by supplying information and technical access necessary for fulfilling regulatory obligations, unless the initial provider had clearly specified that their system was not to be converted into a high‑risk system.[1] Responsibility, then, tracks the actual control and decision‑making regarding how the system is used and transformed, not just the identity of the original model creator.
